extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; citizens and voters considering the proposed Constitution (delegates/informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating normative criteria for structuring the national executive in a written constitution (term length, re-eligibility, pay protection, veto, military and pardoning powers, treaty-making, administration). Focused on constitutional design for the U.S. federal executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of the executive term (four years)
rubrics_metrics.description: A duration of four years, or any other limited duration, would contribute towards firmness and independence of the magistrate without unduly threatening public liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton argues that a four-year term provides a balance: it gives the chief magistrate time to act with firmness, to establish policy and reputation, and for the public to judge his measures before a new election; while being short enough to avoid permanent consolidation of power. The term should be long enough to make the prospect of removal 'sufficiently remote' to enable effective action, yet not so long as to justify alarm about encroachments. Examples and comparative references (British practice) are used to show four years' adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-eligibility of the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-eligibility (the ability of a successful executive to be continued in office) is necessary to give the officer incentive to perform well and to allow the community to retain an effective magistrate when approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-eligibility complements a positive duration by (1) incentivizing good behavior — the hope of continuation rewards merit; (2) permitting the public, after observing performance, to retain a useful administrator; and (3) preserving continuity and accumulated experience in administration. Hamilton contends that schemes permanently or temporarily excluding a former magistrate from future service remove these advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against exclusion (term limits/perpetual disqualification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding a chief magistrate from future service (temporarily or forever) would have pernicious effects outweighing speculative advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton enumerates multiple ill effects of exclusion: (1) diminished inducements to good behavior (less zeal if benefits are known to be temporary); (2) increased temptation to peculation or usurpation by officeholders who know their tenure is fleeting; (3) loss of valuable experience acquired in office; (4) inability to call back experienced leaders in emergencies; (5) constitutional interdiction of administrative stability, causing mutability of measures. He also rebuts the claimed advantages (greater independence, greater security to the people) as equivocal or implausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment and supervision of executive subordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons entrusted with the immediate management of executive matters should be considered the assistants or deputies of the chief magistrate and ought to derive their offices from his appointment (or nomination) and be subject to his superintendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton links the stability of administration to the executive's control over subordinate appointments: if subordinates derive from and answer to the President, continuity of policy and administration is preserved. Frequent turnover of the executive without control of subordinate appointments would cause 'disgraceful and ruinous mutability' in administration as successors reverse predecessors' administrators and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate provision for executive support (compensation protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President shall 'at stated times, receive for his services a compensation WHICH SHALL NEITHER BE INCREASED NOR DIMINISHED DURING THE PERIOD FOR WHICH HE SHALL HAVE BEEN ELECTED; and he SHALL NOT RECEIVE WITHIN THAT PERIOD ANY OTHER EMOLUMENT from the United States, or any of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision prevents the legislature from using salary or emoluments to intimidate or corrupt the executive (by starvation or largesse). Fixing compensation for the term and forbidding other emoluments ensure the executive's financial independence and reduce legislative leverage over his will. Hamilton treats this as indispensable to separation of powers and 'energy' in the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified negative (veto) power of the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: A qualified negative: the President may return bills with objections (a veto), which prevents their becoming laws unless afterwards ratified by two thirds of each legislative house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton defends a qualified veto as both a shield for the Executive against legislative encroachment and as a check against the passage of improper laws produced by faction, haste, or transient passions. He argues the veto increases deliberation and stability in legislation. A qualified (reconsideration) veto is preferred to an absolute veto because it is more likely to be used (less offensive in appearance) and thus more effective in practice; it enables the executive to rally a substantial portion of the legislature to oppose bad measures while being cautious in exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the judiciary distinct from executive revisionary councils
rubrics_metrics.description: The judges should not be combined with the executive in a council for veto/revisionary functions because such association might bias judges or induce them to embark too far in political views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton notes that some states vest a qualified negative in a council including judges, but argues two dangers: (1) judges, as interpreters of law, could be improperly biased if they gave prior political opinions; (2) frequent association with the Executive could draw judges into political combinations, undermining their independence. The guidance is to preserve judicial detachment and avoid corrupting or politicizing the judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized military command in the executive (commander-in-chief)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to be 'commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States WHEN CALLED INTO THE ACTUAL SERVICE of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton argues that direction of war demands qualities best exercised by a single hand: unity and promptness in directing common strength. Thus concentrating military command in the chief magistrate is appropriate and consistent with state precedents; division of this authority would weaken military direction in times of crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power vested in the President (except impeachment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may grant 'reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, EXCEPT IN CASES OF IMPEACHMENT.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton defends a broad pardoning power on grounds of humanity and good policy: the criminal code needs exceptions to avoid excessive severity; a single magistrate is better placed to weigh delicate motives for mercy; and in insurrections or rebellions, the President may need to issue timely pardons to restore tranquility (urgency that legislative concurrence might frustrate). He acknowledges objections about treason but maintains decisive practical reasons for executive discretion in many contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making: President with Senate 'advice and consent' (two-thirds present)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President shall make treaties 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, provided two thirds of the senators present concur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton defends the union of Executive and Senate in treaty-making: treaties are contracts between sovereigns and therefore form a distinct department (neither strictly legislative nor executive). The Executive is the appropriate agent for negotiation, while the Senate's participation safeguards the public interest because treaties operate as laws. He rejects placing treaty power solely in the House or requiring two thirds of all senators (rather than of those present), defending the two-thirds-of-those-present rule as practical and safe for an elective executive of limited duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive right to require written opinions from principal officers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The President may require the opinion, in writing, of the principal officer in each of the executive departments, upon any subject relating to the duties of their respective officers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton treats this provision as largely redundant but nonetheless affirms its existence: the President's right to obtain written advice from principal officers is consistent with executive supervision and administration. It formalizes access to departmental expertise and helps executive accountability in administration.
